idea.title: Why a carousel needed roles instead of generic templates
idea.summary: A Figma visual system had distinct narrative compositions, but the renderer reused generic layouts. Refactoring around explicit editorial roles kept the content model structured while allowing each story moment to have a stable visual treatment.

context.situation: Exported carousel slides shared palette and typography with Figma but did not reproduce its compositions.
context.problem: Generic story and focus layouts repeated panels and treated composition as an optional-field side effect.
context.decision: Add typed Figma-aligned personal roles, map legacy workspace layouts to their closest role, and keep shared slide framing and footer primitives.
context.implementation: Updated the content model contract, workspace adapter, typed renderer data, role layouts, CSS tokens, Studio inspector, validation, and role fixture.
context.result: The live export produced eight 1080 by 1080 slides with Figma-aligned friction, decision, realization, and closing compositions while retaining legacy workspace input support.

learning_points: A visual system often needs role-based compositions rather than one generic template with optional fields.
Keep shared frame and footer primitives while giving each narrative moment its own layout.
Map legacy data deliberately when evolving a renderer contract.
story_points: The mismatch looked like a CSS issue at first.
The root design constraint was that different narrative roles had been collapsed into repeated generic layouts.
The refactor kept workspace data structured and avoided using Figma images as slide backgrounds.
possible_angles: When reusable components make a story look repetitive.
The difference between template reuse and a visual language.

notes: The active workspace carousel was intentionally preserved because it contained unrelated uncommitted content changes.
